name: The Champion Red Pine of Indian Boundary

location.address: Indian Boundary Golf Course, 8600 W Forest Preserve Ave, Chicago, IL 60634 (Forest Preserves of Cook County)

access: Public 18-hole golf course, Forest Preserves of Cook County; a green fee is generally needed to walk the course itself, and whether the tree is visible from a public perimeter path was not confirmed this pass
transport: Metra Milwaukee District West Line to River Grove or Elmwood Park, roughly 20 minutes from Chicago Union Station; or CTA/Pace bus along Forest Preserve Dr/Cumberland Ave. Exact walk time from the nearest stop to the tree was not verified this pass.
verify_notes: Found via the Illinois Big Tree Register (IBTR) feature service, queried statewide for Common_name='red pine': this Indian Boundary Golf Course specimen is the ONLY red pine currently on the register anywhere in Illinois, which makes it the register's default state champion for the species by its own points formula (153.52 pts; circumference 6.8 ft / DBH 26in, height 64 ft, spread 31.5 ft), not a claim we are making ourselves. Measured/listed 2026 (Year_listed_Last_measured field), so the register itself is dated evidence the tree stands now. Nominator: Troy Showerman. Single-source problem: this pass found no independent news or institutional writeup naming this specific tree (the general fpdcc.com Champion Tree Register page describes the PROGRAM, not this entry, and is cited only as context that Forest Preserves of Cook County co-administers champion-tree recognition on its land). The register carries no age field for any species, so age_min/age_max above (50-100 years) is our own inference from typical growth rates for planted red pine reaching a 26in DBH in the Chicago region, not a sourced figure; flag this clearly in the story, do not state a false precision. Red pine (Pinus resinosa) is not native to the Chicago area (it is a more northern species) and this is very likely a planted specimen on golf course grounds, not a wild relict; the remarkable fact is the size/champion status, not antiquity. Access is the open question: Indian Boundary is a public Forest Preserves of Cook County golf course (8600 W Forest Preserve Ave, Chicago 60634, confirmed within Chicago city limits via multiple listings), so a green fee likely applies to walk the fairways; whether the tree can be seen or reached without paying was not established this pass and should be checked, e.g. via the clubhouse or a perimeter trail, before publishing an access claim stronger than 'public course, fee likely applies'.

name: The Kenilworth Witness Oak

location.address: 427 N Kenilworth Ave, Oak Park, IL 60302 (village parkway, Hemingway District)
location.neighbourhood: Oak Park (day trip from Chicago, not within city limits)

access: Free, public parkway tree (the strip of village-owned land between sidewalk and street), viewable from the public right of way; it fronts a private residence so stay on the parkway/sidewalk
transport: CTA Green Line to Oak Park Ave station, roughly 20 to 25 minutes from the Loop, then about a 10 minute walk north; alternatively Metra Union Pacific West Line to Oak Park station
verify_notes: NOT within Chicago city limits: Oak Park is an independent suburb directly west of Chicago, reachable by CTA Green Line in well under the 30-minute day-trip boundary, so it can only ship labelled honestly as Oak Park, IL, never presented as Chicago. Two independent Wednesday Journal (oakpark.com) articles, three years apart, describe the same tree: the 2014 survey piece calls it 'about 230 years old' and 'the oldest parkway tree', identified as a likely Native American Potawatomi Witness Tree marking the route back to the Des Plaines River after a hunt; the 2011 piece, about the Openlands/Morton Arboretum Historic Oak Propagation Project that collected acorns from it in 2008, calls it 'estimated to be three centuries old'. That is a real disagreement (230 vs roughly 300 years) and both figures are given rather than picking a winner, per the flagging rule. Species is bur oak (Quercus macrocarpa) in both sources. It is explicitly called a PARKWAY tree (village-owned strip between sidewalk and street, not private yard), which settles the access question the CLAUDE.md hard rule 10 cares about: this is public land, not someone's front garden. NOT reconfirmed alive since the 2014 article (12 years old); this matters because a sibling Oak Park heritage bur oak on Forest Avenue (244 N Forest Ave, also roughly 200 years old, part of the same heritage-oak cohort) was confirmed DEAD and removed October 2025 (oakpark.com, 'After 200 years, beloved tree sees its last autumn') after developing disease, so heritage oaks of this generation in Oak Park are demonstrably now failing. This is a DIFFERENT tree at a different address, not the Forest Ave one, but the parallel is a real reason for caution: recommend flagging 'alive not reconfirmed since 2014' explicitly in the story and treating this as a strong candidate for a future pass to re-verify in person or via a 2025/2026 source before it ships, rather than shipping on 12-year-old sourcing alone. Location precision is 'approximate' because we have a street address (geocoded via OpenStreetMap Nominatim to the building footprint, not a surveyed tree point) rather than tree-level coordinates; a parkway tree is typically a few metres from that point, not exact.
